similar_scenes.name: Synthpop británico
similar_scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
similar_scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
similar_scenes.desc: Con The Human League a la cabeza, el auge de 1981-1982: los sintetizadores baratos (el Wasp), las cajas de ritmos Linn y las baterías Simmons democratizan la electrónica, al punto de que el sindicato de músicos propone racionarlos. Instrumento andrógino frente a la guitarra fálica, refugio para los adolescentes que se sentían distintos. Soft Cell lleva la sordidez neoyorquina de Suicide a Leeds («Tainted Love», «Bedsitter», Non-Stop Erotic Cabaret); Japan, máscaras de dandi de Catford, pasa del glam desfasado a la belleza escultural de «Ghosts»; OMD, Pete Shelley («Homosapien»), y Depeche Mode, de chicos inocentes de Basildon en Mute a la política y el sadomasoquismo de «Everything Counts» y «Master and Servant». Hacia 1983 el diluvio de grupos mediocres provoca la reacción y vuelven las guitarras.

podcast.title: Alternative Name for Technopop
podcast.body: This term was also an acceptable alternative name for the genre known as Technopop during its original emergence. "although synthpop was also acceptable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Chicago House Music Influence
podcast.body: Synthpop influences later migrated to Chicago, becoming an integral part of the development and rise of house music in the city. "In North America, synth pop influences settled in Chicago, where the sounds became integral to the rise of house music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Elvis Costello's Image Re-upholstered
podcast.body: The success of Elvis Costello's "Every Day I Write The Book" on MTV helped him become "conversant with MTV, re-apholstering his image for the synth pop age." This adaptation allowed him to remain relevant and achieve chart success during the genre's dominance. "It also made Costello conversant with MTV, re-apholstering his image for the synth pop age."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Emergence in the 80s
podcast.body: In 1982, music videos became slicker, glossier, and more expensive, leading to a shift in the sound of new wave from powerpop and post-punk to synthpop. This marked a "changing of the guard" moment in popular music, with bands like The Human League exemplifying the new aesthetic. "They were changing the very sound of new wave from Powerpop and Postpunk to Synthpop."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Joe Jackson's MTV Staple
podcast.body: Joe Jackson's "Steppin' Out" video became an MTV staple "at the peak of 80s synth pop." This success helped reinvent his career, demonstrating the genre's commercial power and its ability to elevate artists to mainstream prominence. "The video became an MTV staple at the peak of 80s synth pop."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Joe Jackson's Smooth Jazz on Radio
podcast.body: At the height of synthpop in the summer of 1984, Joe Jackson successfully integrated smooth jazz elements into his music, with "You Can't Get What You Want (Till You Know What You Want)" reaching number 15. This demonstrated an interesting crossover and broadened the sonic palette heard on radio during the synthpop era. "at the height of synth pop, Joe Jackson was getting smooth jazz on the radio."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: MTV Programming Staple
podcast.body: Its stylish nature made it perfectly suited for MTV upon its August 1981 launch. British synthpop acts provided a significant source of programming for the new channel due to their extensive backlog of performance videos. "And they were all very stylish which was perfect because there was this new thing called MTV. And it needed to be fit. See when MTV first went on the air in August of 1981, they had a grand total of 250 videos, most of which were from Britain. So the UK had this long history of bands performing on TV, so they had a big backlog of stuff to choose from. So until North American record labels in bands started investing in making videos, a big source of programming for MTV were clips from these stylish synth pop bands from the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Prevalence of Two-Person Model
podcast.body: Many bands in this genre, especially from the UK, commonly featured a two-person lineup: a singer or front person and a composer/programmer/operator. "Many of them had this two-person model. You had the singer or front person and at the back, the composer, programmer, operator."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Synthpop / Technopop – Guitars Out, Electronics In; Filled the Post-Disco Dance Void
podcast.body: Synthpop (also called Technopop) emerged as one of the biggest offshoots of New Wave, based on the idea that guitars were out and electronics were the future. It was also extremely danceable, filling the post-disco dance void that had been created when disco was deemed uncool. Devo (from Akron, Ohio, supported by David Bowie) were among the original synthpop pioneers, and keyboard-focused UK acts like Depeche Mode, Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, and Soft Cell pushed the sound further. "For practitioners and fans, guitars were out. The future was all about electronics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
